This is the only product that I purchase where the supposed purpose of tariffs beyond just another way for government to grab some of our earnings - that is, as an incentive for domestic manufacturing to sprout up in the face of foreign based competitors that have less overhead - has actually occurred. Since post-covid when I did a big reduction in any kind of alcoholic beverages, Topo Chico "Twist of Lime" sparkling water has been my go to, apart from coffee. And for the past year this bottled in Mexico staple has been for the most part inexplicably stripped off of the shelves. Luckily HEB, which anyone that has ever gone into one, is already aware that is the greatest grocery chain in all of the USA (by far!) - came out with their own brand version of it, bottled here in Tejas, that is pretty close to the original.
So, good news, there were some jobs created in expanding an already existing bottling plant. But what tariffs have failed to do is expand domestic manufacturing in so many areas, especially electronics, given that the investment, materials, time and brain trust needed to create plants for these is just way more substantial than what you need to make flavored fizzy water. Tariffs ironically also seriously undermine building new infrastructures here, because it inflates the costs of materials or parts that are imported needed to create these. So now I get to read the news about how parts like THAT VCA's and 5532 opamps that help create the analog audio production tools the so called "industry" I work in are being discontinued one by one - as well as see evidence that the USA's "global soft power" that to date has protected Taiwan, where the vast majority of advanced chips are manufactured, is being eroded, to the point that the timeline where they could be swallowed up by the PRC is getting shortened, all the while incentives to create chip manufacturing here (e.g. the "Chips Act") are being discontinued because the name attached to those things were from previous admin's, rather than the Narcissist in Chief's.
Bottom line is most folks in the USA have majorly benefited by living in a globalized economy that have enabled the USA to be the recipient at a major discount, of tons of goods, as well as commodities that we finish into goods - but tariffs, trade wars, and beefs at long time allies for no reason, have helped shoot that pooch. Can we get back to the standing we used to have by eliminating them after a shift in who controls our gov? Not likely, but we can and should do better than we are doing now, that is for sure. In the meantime, at least if you are in Texas like me, you can enjoy some made in TX fizzy water.

🚨 TRUMP PROMISES AMERICANS A $5,000 “DIVIDEND” IF REPUBLICANS KEEP CONGRESS — BUT WHO PAYS FOR IT?

DALLAS — September 10, 2026 — President Donald Trump has made an extraordinary promise less than two months before the U.S. midterm elections:

If Republicans retain control of both the House and Senate on November 3, Trump says he wants to send **$5,000 to every adult American citizen**.

Trump unveiled the proposal Wednesday night at the Republican Party’s first-ever midterm convention in Dallas, calling the payment the:

**“Trump Dividend.”**

His condition was unmistakably political:

Republicans must keep control of Congress.

Trump also said the money would have to be **spent inside the United States**. But he gave no detailed explanation of where the enormous amount of money would come from or how the program would work.

## THE PRICE TAG: MORE THAN $1 TRILLION

This would not be a small stimulus program.

Reuters estimates that if approximately 270 million U.S. adults received $5,000 each, the total cost would reach roughly:

**$1.35 trillion.**

The actual figure could be lower depending on eligibility because Trump specifically referred to adult citizens, and Vice President JD Vance later suggested wealthy Americans might not receive the payment.

But even with exclusions, the cost would likely remain enormous.

For comparison, the United States is already running an annual federal budget deficit of nearly:

**$1.8 trillion.**

And the national debt recently passed:

**$40 trillion.**

Adding another trillion-dollar federal payment would therefore immediately raise questions about borrowing, inflation and the sustainability of government finances.

## TRUMP DIDN’T SAY WHERE THE MONEY WOULD COME FROM

Trump described the payment as a dividend generated by America’s economic success.

But he did not provide a financing plan.

Within an hour of Trump’s announcement, Vice President JD Vance suggested that **tariff revenues** could help fund the payments.

There is a major mathematical problem with that explanation.

According to the Associated Press, the amount required for the proposed dividends would **far exceed the tariff revenue collected by the federal government**.

So unless eligibility is dramatically restricted or another funding source is found, Congress would have to identify hundreds of billions — potentially more than $1 trillion — from somewhere else.

That could mean:

• higher government borrowing
• spending cuts elsewhere
• new taxes or revenue
• or some combination of all three

So far, no detailed legislation has been released.

## CAN TRUMP JUST SEND THE CHECKS HIMSELF?

No.

Despite Trump previously suggesting presidents may have broad authority over similar payments, the $5,000 program would require congressional authorization or congressional cooperation.

That is one reason the promise is tied so closely to Republicans maintaining control of both chambers.

Republican Senator Bernie Moreno has already said he intends to prepare legislation so the “Trump Dividend” could be passed immediately after the November election if Republicans win.

So voters should understand an important distinction:

**Trump has made a campaign promise.**

He has not created a $5,000 payment program.

No checks have been authorized.

No funding has been approved.

And no final eligibility rules currently exist.

## IS THIS LITERALLY “BUYING VOTES”?

Critics immediately described the promise as vote-buying.

Politically, it is easy to understand why.

Trump is effectively telling voters:

**Keep Republicans in power, and you could receive $5,000.**

But legally, the situation is more complicated.

An attorney consulted by the Associated Press said the proposal would not necessarily violate election laws because individual voters would not receive money in exchange for proving that they personally voted Republican.

The payment would instead be a government program available to qualifying Americans regardless of whether they voted Republican, Democratic, for another party — or did not vote at all.

That makes it fundamentally different from directly paying an individual for their vote.

Whether the eventual structure could face other legal challenges would depend on how Congress writes the legislation.

## THE TIMING IS IMPOSSIBLE TO IGNORE

Trump did not announce the proposal during a White House economic briefing.

He announced it at a **Republican midterm convention**, during an event specifically designed to help Republicans retain control of Congress.

Trump even urged voters to behave as though **he himself were on the ballot**.

Republicans currently face a difficult electoral environment.

Several GOP candidates in competitive races skipped the Dallas convention, while polling shows widespread dissatisfaction with the cost of living and the continuing war with Iran.

Trump’s approval ratings have also fallen sharply.

That makes the $5,000 announcement more than an economic proposal.

It is now part of the Republican Party’s strategy for winning the November midterms.

## AND THEN THERE’S THE INFLATION QUESTION

Sending enormous amounts of cash into the economy can boost consumer spending.

That is partly the point.

But if consumer demand increases faster than the economy’s ability to produce goods and services, prices can also rise.

The United States experienced a similar debate after the massive stimulus packages issued during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Those payments were introduced during an economic emergency.

Trump’s proposed dividend would arrive under very different circumstances — while the federal government is already running a huge deficit and carrying more than $40 trillion in debt.

That does not automatically mean a $5,000 payment would cause another inflation surge.

But a program potentially exceeding $1 trillion would be large enough that its economic consequences could not simply be ignored.

## THE “TRUMP DIVIDEND” HAS CHANGED BEFORE

Trump has previously floated the idea of returning government revenue directly to Americans.

Earlier in 2026, he proposed a smaller:

**$2,000 dividend.**

That proposal was never implemented.

Now the amount has jumped to:

**$5,000.**

And for the first time, Trump has explicitly linked the payment to Republicans winning an election.

That is what makes Wednesday’s announcement so politically unusual.

## CIVICOHUB FACT CHECK

**Has Trump promised $5,000 to every adult American citizen?**

YES.

Trump publicly announced the proposal at the Republican convention in Dallas.

**Will Americans definitely receive $5,000?**

NO.

There is currently no approved program, no enacted legislation and no detailed funding mechanism.

**Is receiving the money conditional on an individual voting Republican?**

NO.

Trump tied implementation of the program to Republicans controlling Congress, not to how an individual recipient personally votes.

**Would Congress have to approve it?**

YES.

Congressional action would be required to authorize such a massive federal payment.

**Can tariff revenue currently cover the entire proposal?**

NO.

Available tariff revenues are nowhere near enough to finance a universal $5,000 payment costing potentially more than $1 trillion.

**Could it add to the national debt?**

YES — unless Congress finds sufficient spending cuts or additional revenue to pay for it.

## THE BOTTOM LINE

This is not yet a government benefit.

It is an election promise.

And it is an extraordinary one.

Less than two months before Americans decide control of Congress, the president is telling voters that a Republican victory could produce a **$5,000 payment for every qualifying adult citizen**.

Potential price tag:

**More than $1 trillion.**

Current national debt:

**More than $40 trillion.**

Detailed funding plan:

**None announced.**

Congressional approval:

**Still required.**

Trump calls it a dividend from America’s economic success.

His critics will inevitably call it something else.

But before deciding what to call it, there is a simpler question voters deserve answered:

**Where does the $5,000 come from?**

Until the White House and Congress provide that answer, the “Trump Dividend” remains a campaign promise — not a check in the mail.

Sources: Reuters, Associated Press, NOS — September 9–10, 2026.

Plug in solar arrives in time for the end of summer

A Small Change That Could Make a Big Difference

27 August 2026 marked an important milestone for home energy in the UK. Compliant plug-in solar systems are now legal across Great Britain, allowing households to generate electricity simply by plugging an approved solar kit into a standard socket. For many people, particularly those in flats, rented homes, or properties unsuitable for rooftop solar, this is the first realistic opportunity to generate their own renewable electricity.

Plug-in solar is not just for homeowners. Flats, rented properties and community buildings now have options that simply didn’t exist before.

Unlike traditional rooftop solar, plug-in systems are designed to be simple. A typical kit consists of one or two solar panels connected to a micro-inverter, producing up to 800W of AC power. The new regulations allow certified systems to be connected directly to a household socket without the need for an electrician, provided all safety requirements are met. Only approved, certified kits qualify, and there is currently a limit of one device per household. Note that people need to notify their grid operator (DNO) within 28 days of installing a plug-in solar system, so the network operators know how much power is flowing around, and how demand might change. Currently you can do this easily on this website https://myplugin.solar/

What Can You Save?

The Government estimates that an 800W system could provide up to 20% of an average home’s electricity use and save up to £110 per year. Actual savings depend heavily on how much electricity you use during daylight hours. Homes occupied during the day, or those with continuously running appliances such as fridges, broadband routers, home offices, aquariums or heat pumps, are likely to see the greatest benefit. It’s also worth noting that 800W is the maximum hte panels are allowed to export, so it’s possible some will be 1000W or even more as actual output will be less unless they are angles to the sun correctly.

Current retail pricing suggests entry-level systems start at around £599, with larger systems costing more. At the lower end of the market, a £599 system saving £80 to £110 annually would have a simple payback period of roughly five to eight years. Given that solar panels typically last 25 years or more, the lifetime return could be substantial.

For many households, however, the attraction is not purely financial. Plug-in solar offers a low-cost entry point into renewable energy without scaffolding, roof work, planning complications or significant upfront expense.

Who Benefits Most?

These systems are particularly attractive for people living in flats with balconies, households with suitable garden space or south-facing walls, renters who cannot install conventional rooftop solar. Home workers or anyone who can consume more the generated electricity during daylight hours when it’s being produced will achieve the greatest savings.

Germany’s experience demonstrates the potential. Millions of Europeans have already adopted similar “balcony solar” systems, creating a mature market that has helped shape the UK’s new regulatory framework.

The Risks and Limitations

Plug-in solar is not a miracle solution and there are some important caveats.

The maximum permitted output is 800W, meaning these systems will only cover a fraction of the energy needs of most households. Government estimates suggest around 20% of an average home’s electricity consumption under favourable conditions.

Batteries are currently excluded from the new plug-in framework. Energy generated during sunny periods needs to be used at the time it is produced, otherwise some of it may be exported to the grid without financial reward. However, batteries are probalby coming (and there’s little to stop people who know what they are doing to use a battery, though at their own risk).

Consumers should also note that only approved products may be used, extension leads and adaptors are prohibited, mounting systems must be robust enough to withstand adverse weather, and leasehold or planning restrictions may still apply depending on the installation location.

What About Export Payments?

One of the biggest opportunities is being paid for exporting uneused electricity. At this point export is allowed, but you will not be paid for it.

The good news is that progress is being made. Both Octopus Energy and Fuse Energy have publicly indicated that they are working on mechanisms to allow plug-in solar users to access export payments. According to recent reporting, Octopus intends to make its existing Outgoing Octopus tariff, currently paying 12p/kWh, available once registration arrangements are clarified. Fuse Energy has also confirmed it is developing an export solution, although details have not yet been announced.We do know it pays its existing customers 13p/kWh however.

For most households, however, export income is likely to remain secondary. The greatest value still comes from using the electricity yourself and avoiding importing power from the grid.

The Bigger Picture

Plug-in solar is unlikely to replace conventional rooftop solar. What it does offer is something arguably more important: accessibility. For hundreds of thousands of households previously excluded from home generation, it provides a low-cost, low-risk way to participate in the energy transition and reduce household bills.

It is also a reminder that reducing energy costs rarely depends on a single measure. Plug-in solar can make a useful contribution, but households should also look at improving insulation, switching to LED lighting, reducing standby consumption and optimising heating controls.

Flick the switch

Energy tariffs matter too. At the time of writing, one of the simplest, no cost opportunities for many households may be switching gas supplier. Fuse Energy, for example, currently offers one of the lowest gas standing charges around, combined with a very competitive rate per kWh if gas used. For homes with relatively modest gas usage, standing charges can account for a significant proportion of annual costs. In many cases switching will save £50 per year on the standing charge. Even better, there is often a switching credit, worth as much again (or more)

If you do switch before 18 Sep and use referral code SIMON82967 you’ll receive £100 and Sustainable Ferriby CIC will benefit too https://www.fuseenergy.com/app


Combining a competitive tariff with sensible energy efficiency measures and a plug-in solar system could reduce household energy bills by considerably more than any single intervention on its own.

Win:Win:Win

The arrival of plug-in solar may not transform Britain’s energy system overnight, but it removes a barrier that has excluded many households from generating their own clean electricity. For a relatively modest investment, it offers a practical first step towards greater energy independence, lower bills and lower carbon emissions.

🚨 WHY CANADA WALKED AWAY: U.S. TRADE DEMANDS REACHED FAR BEYOND TARIFFS

WASHINGTON/OTTAWA — August 24, 2026 — The collapse of trade negotiations between the United States and Canada was not simply a dispute over whether a tariff should be 15%, 25% or 50%.

By the final hours of negotiations, the disagreement had expanded into something much bigger:

**Who gets to determine Canada’s trade policy, industrial strategy — and even protections for its French language and culture?**

Less than two days before negotiations collapsed, Canadian Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc emerged from talks in Washington saying:

**“We’re very close.”**

The two countries had made substantial progress.

Washington was considering major tariff relief for Canadian autos, steel and aluminum.

Canada was prepared to remove remaining retaliatory tariffs on key American products and encourage provinces to return U.S. alcohol to store shelves.

Then, according to Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, the United States introduced new terms.

Canada rejected them.

And the deal collapsed.

## THIS WASN’T JUST ABOUT CARS

Automobiles were one of the biggest economic disputes.

Canada wanted significantly lower U.S. tariffs on Canadian-made vehicles.

But the two sides disagreed over how much Canadian and other North American content inside those vehicles should qualify for favorable treatment.

That matters enormously because the U.S. and Canadian automotive industries do not operate as separate systems.

Parts routinely cross the border several times during production.

A transmission, battery component or other part may contain Canadian, American and Mexican content before the finished vehicle ever reaches a dealership.

But the dispute did not stop with automobiles.

## CANADA SAYS THE U.S. WANTED MORE CONTROL OVER ITS TRADE POLICY

One of the most consequential issues concerned Canada’s ability to pursue its own relationships with other countries.

Recent reporting indicates that U.S. demands would have constrained Canada’s freedom over future trade arrangements and pushed Ottawa toward greater alignment with Washington’s trade policies toward third countries.

That is particularly important because Carney is deliberately pursuing the opposite strategy.

Canada is trying to become **less dependent on the United States**.

Over the past year, Ottawa says it has signed more than 20 trade and security agreements across five continents.

Canada is expanding negotiations with India and ASEAN and plans deeper economic discussions with the European Union.

Carney says Canadian businesses already have tariff-free access to markets representing around **1.5 billion consumers** — and he wants to dramatically increase that number.

Accepting restrictions on Canada’s ability to negotiate independently with other countries would therefore strike directly at one of Carney’s central economic policies.

His government described maintaining Canada’s:

**“flexibility, independence, and sovereignty”**

as one of its core objectives in the U.S. negotiations.

And on that point, Canada refused to move.

## THEN CAME FRENCH LANGUAGE AND CANADIAN CULTURE

This is one of the least discussed — but perhaps most revealing — parts of the failed negotiations.

Carney says the United States also pressed Canada over protections involving:

**the French language and Canadian culture.**

And unlike some of the disputed details surrounding the negotiations, this comes directly from Carney himself.

In his official statement explaining why Canada abandoned the talks, Carney said:

**“We were not prepared to compromise on the protection of the French language and our culture.”**

Then he added something even more significant:

**“For my government and for Canada, these issues were never on the table, even though the United States tried until the very last minute.”**

The full text of the American proposal has not been made public.

That means it would be wrong to claim that Trump demanded Canada “abolish French-language protections” or end all Canadian cultural rules.

There is currently not enough public evidence to make such a specific claim.

But Canada’s prime minister has explicitly confirmed that Washington sought concessions concerning **French-language and cultural protections** — and that Ottawa refused.

For Canada, these are not minor commercial regulations.

French is one of the country’s two official languages.

Protection of Canadian and French-language media and culture has been embedded in Canadian policy for decades, particularly because Canada shares a massive media market with the United States.

For Ottawa, that made this a question of national identity as much as economics.

## CARNEY: “THEY ASKED TOO MUCH AND OFFERED TOO LITTLE”

Carney says that earlier in the week he believed a mutually beneficial agreement was within reach.

Then the American proposal changed.

According to the Canadian prime minister, the new terms were:

**“uneconomic, unfair”**

and undermined the benefits Canada expected to receive from the agreement.

His summary was unusually blunt:

**“They asked too much and offered too little.”**

Late Friday, Carney ordered Canadian negotiators to leave Washington and return to Ottawa.

The negotiations were suspended.

## BUT WASHINGTON DISPUTES CANADA’S VERSION

There are two sides to this breakdown.

The Trump administration says Canada — not the United States — prevented the agreement.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer called the collapse:

**“a missed opportunity for Canada.”**

A senior Trump administration official told Reuters that Washington had offered Canada what would have been the most favorable tariff treatment available to any major exporter to the United States.

According to the U.S. account, Canada then demanded additional concessions involving:

• steel and aluminum
• autos
• softwood lumber
• other strategic sectors

Washington therefore argues that **Canada moved the goalposts**.

Ottawa says exactly the opposite:

**The United States changed the conditions at the last minute.**

The actual final negotiating texts have not been publicly released, so some details cannot yet be independently resolved.

That distinction matters.

But what is no longer disputed is that negotiations which appeared close to completion on Thursday were dead by Friday night.

## THEN THE TARIFFS HIT

After the deal collapsed, the United States imposed **50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion worth of Canadian products**.

The affected goods represent only a portion of Canada's enormous export relationship with the United States, but some individual industries could suffer substantial damage.

Canada responded by promising **dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs beginning September 8**, targeting sectors including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics.

Then Trump escalated again.

On Monday, he threatened to impose **50% tariffs on Canadian-made cars, trucks and auto parts beginning January 1, 2027**.

That measure has not yet taken effect.

But the threat dramatically raises the stakes.

## THIS IS BECOMING A FIGHT OVER SOVEREIGNTY

Trump has repeatedly argued that Canada benefits disproportionately from access to the American economy and that manufacturers can avoid tariffs by simply moving production into the United States.

Canada sees the situation very differently.

Carney says economic integration with the United States is increasingly being used as leverage to force Canadian concessions.

His response is now becoming a defining feature of Canadian economic policy:

**reduce dependence on America.**

Ottawa is looking toward Europe, India, ASEAN and other international markets while investing heavily in domestic industry, defense, energy and infrastructure.

Carney’s message is essentially that access to the U.S. market is enormously valuable — but not valuable enough to surrender Canada’s ability to determine its own policies.

And on Monday, the rhetoric escalated further.

Trump told Canada to **“fall in line.”**

Carney responded that Canada would negotiate with the United States as a sovereign equal — not as a subordinate.

## CIVICOHUB FACT CHECK

Did the U.S.–Canada negotiations collapse only because of tariffs?

**No.**

Tariffs on autos, steel, aluminum and other products were major components of the negotiations, but Canada says the final disagreement extended into its broader economic sovereignty.

Did the United States demand that Canada completely stop trading with other countries?

**There is no public evidence supporting that broad claim.**

However, reporting indicates that Washington sought restrictions affecting Canada’s freedom over future trade arrangements and its trade policy toward third countries.

The complete American negotiating text has not been released.

Did French language protections really become part of the dispute?

**Yes.**

Carney explicitly stated that Canada refused to compromise on protections for the French language and Canadian culture and said the United States continued pressing the issue until the final stage of negotiations.

Did Canada refuse every compromise?

**No.**

Canada says it was prepared to remove remaining retaliatory tariffs in strategic sectors, encourage provinces to restore American alcohol sales and make administrative concessions involving supply management in exchange for substantial U.S. tariff reductions.

Did Washington think it was offering Canada a good deal?

**Yes.**

The Trump administration says its offer would have provided Canada with exceptionally favorable access to the American market and accuses Ottawa of demanding additional concessions.

## THE BOTTOM LINE

This trade deal did not collapse because the two countries never got close.

They did.

On Thursday:

**“We’re very close.”**

By Friday night:

**Negotiations were over.**

The final disagreement had expanded far beyond tariff percentages.

Autos mattered.

Steel mattered.

Aluminum mattered.

But so did something more fundamental:

**Canada’s right to decide its own trade relationships.**

**Canada’s right to protect its French language and culture.**

**And Canada’s unwillingness to exchange those powers for preferential access to the American market.**

Washington says Canada walked away from an exceptionally favorable offer.

Ottawa says Washington transformed a trade agreement into a demand for concessions Canada could not accept as a sovereign country.

Without the full negotiating documents, not every disputed detail can yet be independently verified.

But Carney has made Canada's red line unmistakably clear:

**Lower tariffs were negotiable.**

**Canadian sovereignty was not.**

Sources: Prime Minister of Canada, Reuters, Associated Press — August 20–24, 2026.

This is a little experiment in using an LLM to validate or invalidate motivations.

It is widely reported that Mr Trump and his associates made money in the stock exchange, through advance knowledge of the war winding down or heating up. That’s unproven: only one person has been charged, and he hasn’t come to trial.

However, we can take the motivation instead, and ask if there is a similar one, and opportunity to profit, in the applying and retracting of tariffs. That’s the kind of discussion that an LLM can look for in their training data. Therefor I asked Claude to tell me about opportunities to profit from advance warning of tariff changes. It replied:

I did find substantial reporting about alleged insider trading tied to tariff announcements, which is relevant to your question.

Profit Opportunities from Advance Knowledge of Tariff Decisions

If someone had advance knowledge of when Trump would apply, remove, or modify tariffs, several trading strategies would present profit opportunities:

Direct Equity Trading

Stock price movements around tariff announcements create straightforward opportunities. Sectors affected by tariffs (steel, automotive, agriculture, manufacturing) would experience predictable price swings. Someone with advance knowledge could short stocks (bet on price declines) before tariff announcements drive prices down, or purchase calls/puts (options contracts betting on specific price movements) to capture gains when prices reverse after tariff pauses.

Options Trading

Options provide leveraged exposure with minimal upfront capital. The reported cases show investors purchasing call options minutes before tariff pause announcements—betting that the market would rise—yielding returns in the tens of millions of dollars within hours. Short-dated options on indices like the S&P 500 become extremely valuable if you know a market-moving announcement is imminent.

Commodity and Currency Hedging

Tariffs directly affect commodity prices. Steel, aluminum, and agricultural commodities move sharply on tariff news. Similarly, currency markets react to trade policy announcements. Advance knowledge would allow positioning in commodity futures or forex markets before prices shift.

Targeted Sector Plays

Industries facing new tariffs would see immediate declines, while competitors or alternatives would see gains. For example, domestic steel producers benefit while foreign competitors are hurt. Investors with advance notice could position accordingly across entire industry groups.

The Reversal Strategy

The most suspicious pattern in the reporting involves tariff announcements followed by reversals. Someone could profit twice: first by shorting the market when tariffs are announced (knowing a reversal is coming), then immediately switching to calls or long positions before the pause announcement, capturing gains in both directions.

Interestingly, Congressman Steven Horsford had noticed evidence of tariff manipulation:

The Evidence

Congressman Steven Horsford documented suspicious trading patterns around Trump tariff announcements: 18 minutes before a tariff pause announcement, traders placed enormous bets that markets would surge, and 47 minutes before an Iran negotiations announcement, someone shorted the oil market by hundreds of millions of dollars. U.S. House of Representatives

More specifically, on April 9, 2025, 5,105 call option contracts betting the S&P 500 would rise traded at roughly $4.20 each (a $2.1 million investment) just 18 minutes before Trump's tariff pause announcement. These options exploded to over $30 million in value within 24 hours. upriseri.com

The pattern repeated during Trump's first administration: investor Carl Icahn sold $31 million in steel-related stocks days before Trump announced steel tariffs in 2018, saving approximately $2 million in losses. upriseri.com

Indonesia fails to stop importation of goods made with forced labor: USTR

Indonesia Included in USTR Findings and Proposes Action in Investigations into Failures to Take Action on Trade in Goods Made with Forced Labor

USTR Makes Findings and Proposes Action in 60 Section 301 Investigations Relating to Failures to Take Action on Trade in Forced Labor Goods

On June 02, 2026, the U. S. Trade Representative (USTR) issued a decision “under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 that the acts … of 60 economies related to the failure to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor is unreasonable and burdens or restricts U.S. commerce, and are thus actionable under Section 301(b) of the Trade Act.”

“USTR has prepared a comprehensive report, Acts, Policies, and Practices of Various Economies Related to the Failure to Impose and Effectively Enforce a Prohibition on the Importation of Goods Produced with Forced Labor, that supports the findings in each investigation.”

The USTR decided that “the failure of each of the 60 investigated economies to impose and effectively enforce a forced labor import prohibition is unreasonable or discriminatory and burdens or restricts U.S. commerce, and thus is actionable under Section 301(b)(1) of the Trade Act.”

“In particular, the U.S. Trade Representative determined:

  • The following 54 economies have failed to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor: Algeria; Angola; Argentina; Australia; the Bahamas; Bahrain; Bangladesh; Brazil; Cambodia; Chile; China, People’s Republic of; Colombia; Costa Rica; Dominican Republic; Egypt; El Salvador; Guatemala; Guyana; Honduras; Hong Kong, China; India; Iraq; Israel; Japan; Jordan; Kazakhstan; Kuwait; Libya; Malaysia; Morocco; New Zealand; Nicaragua; Nigeria; Norway; Oman; Peru; the Philippines; Qatar; Russia; Saudi Arabia; Singapore; South Africa; South Korea; Sri Lanka; Switzerland; Taiwan; Thailand; Trinidad and Tobago; Türkiye; United Arab Emirates; United Kingdom; Uruguay; Venezuela; and Vietnam.
  • The following six economies have failed to effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor: Canada; Ecuador, the European Union; Indonesia; Mexico; and Pakistan.”

According to the decision, “The failure of each of the investigated economies to impose and effectively enforce a forced labor import prohibition is unreasonable because it: (1) undermines the universal aim of eliminating forced labor; (2) permits firms that avail themselves of forced labor to produce goods at lower cost and thereby distort market conditions for firms that do not use forced labor; (3) undermines the profitability of firms that do not use forced labor; and (4) contributes to the circumvention of existing forced labor import prohibitions.”

“The failure of each of the above-listed economies to impose and effectively enforce a forced labor import prohibition burdens or restricts U.S. commerce by subjecting U.S. producers to unfair competition from forced labor goods both in export markets and the U.S. market, and by displacing foreign goods produced without forced labor or forced labor inputs into the United States and other markets.”

Call for written comment

“The U.S. Trade Representative has also determined to propose responsive actions in these investigations. As set out in the Federal Register notice, the public is invited to provide written comments by July 6, 2026, on the proposed actions.”

Hearings into failure to enforce ban on goods produced using forced labor

USTR will hold hearings about the proposed actions on July 7, 2026. As set out in the Federal Register notice, interested persons are invited to submit requests to appear at the hearing by June 22.”

Indonesia–China partnership more fragile than it appears

By Klaus Heinrich Raditio, Driyarkara School of Philosophy, and Ardhitya Eduard Yeremia, Universitas Indonesia, East Asia Forum, East Asian Bureau of Economic Research (EABER), April 28, 2026

During the presidency of Joko Widodo, China became more central to Indonesia than at any point in the past. Widodo left office with China as Indonesia’s second-largest source of foreign investment. China also emerged as the largest export destination for Indonesia’s nickel-processing hubs that supported Indonesia’s ambition to build a downstream mineral industry.

Through these developments, Widodo transformed the Indonesia–China comprehensive strategic partnership from a largely diplomatic symbol into one underpinned by significant economic cooperation.

This impression appeared to deepen during the first year of Prabowo Subianto’s presidency. Jakarta seemed open to Beijing’s proposal for joint development in the South China Sea through a controversial joint statement. A 2+2 dialogue mechanism was established between their foreign and defence ministries in April 2025. Two months later, they inaugurated an integrated electric-vehicle battery manufacturing centre in Indonesia. Against this backdrop, some observers began to argue that Indonesia was ‘sleepwalking into strategic alignment with China’.

Yet the trajectory appeared to shift in the second year Prabowo’s presidency. In July 2025, the framework for a US–Indonesian reciprocal trade agreement was announced, with the Agreement on Reciprocal Trade signed in February 2026. Under the arrangement, US tariffs on Indonesian goods would decrease from 32 per cent to 19 per cent. Though the reduction was welcomed, the agreement was widely perceived in Indonesia as unfair. The decision raised questions about Indonesia’s bargaining power in negotiations with Washington while also casting uncertainty over the future of Indonesia–China strategic relations.

Three provisions of the agreement are particularly notable.

Article 3.3 on digital trade stipulates Indonesia must communicate with the United States before entering into a new digital trade agreement with another country that could jeopardize essential US interests. It represents a clear attempt by Washington to constrain Indonesia’s cooperation with China in the digital economy. China’s Digital Silk Road already has a strong presence in Southeast Asia, and Indonesia is among its key destinations in the region with Chinese firms accounting for 44 per cent of Indonesia’s e-commerce market.

Article 5.1 requires Indonesia adopt equivalently restrictive measures if the United States imposes trade restrictions on imports from a ‘third country’ for economic or national security reasons. This clause could constrain Indonesia’s economic engagement with China — Washington’s principal strategic competitor.

Article 6.1 deals with critical minerals. It requires Indonesia to restrict foreign-owned processing facilities’ excess production by ensuring conformity with Indonesia’s mining quota. And it bars foreign-owned industrial parks and processing facilities from receiving preferential legal entitlements.

While the language of ‘foreign-owned’ is nominally neutral, it obscures a specific reality — a substantial majority of Indonesia’s nickel processing facilities are backed by Chinese capital. The industrial parks in Morowali, Weda Bay and elsewhere were built on Chinese investment — the very foundation of the economic partnership that Widodo cultivated. Article 6.1 effectively subjects that foundation to new restrictions negotiated not with Beijing but with Washington.

Collectively, these provisions of the agreement restrict a wide spectrum of Indonesia’s engagement with China. Despite the comprehensive strategic partnership supposedly being at its strongest, Jakarta obliged to the provisions. Indeed, by agreeing to controversial provisions that could potentially target a ‘third country’, Indonesia appears willing to disregard China’s strategic interests.

This highlights a key difference between Widodo and Prabowo in managing relations with major powers. Widodo maintained close engagement with China but not necessarily at the expense of US–Indonesian relations. By contrast, Prabowo appears to accommodate US interests in a manner that risks undermining Indonesia’s strong engagement with China, albeit incidentally.

Despite the positive trajectory of the post-Suharto era and Widodo’s further deepening of economic ties, Indonesia–China relations still rest on a fragile foundation.

On the Chinese side, Beijing frequently emphasises multilateralism and engagement with the Global South, including through its vision of a ‘community of shared future’. Yet if China seeks to maintain Indonesia as a key partner amid growing geopolitical competition, it must ensure that the relationship rests on deeper and more solid foundations. Korea’s semiconductor exports are on a tear, with the first 10 days of the month tracking near 90% YoY growth. This level of expansion has historically been associated with semiconductor index levels that are 50-60% above current trading levels, according to Andreas Steno Larsen. While this may seem like a remarkable feat, it’s important to consider the broader context and potential implications for the industry as a whole.

Firstly, it’s worth noting that Korea has long been a major player in the global semiconductor market, with companies such as Samsung and SK Hynix dominating the landscape. However, the current growth spurt could be seen as a sign of increased competition and innovation within the industry, as well as the growing demand for semiconductors across various sectors.

One potential factor driving this growth is the increasing adoption of advanced technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI), the Internet of Things (IoT), and 5G network infrastructure. As more devices become connected to the internet, there will be a greater need for powerful and efficient semiconductors to support these applications. Additionally, the ongoing development of new manufacturing processes and materials could lead to further improvements in performance and cost-effectiveness, potentially fueling even more growth in the future.

However, it’s important to recognize that this rapid expansion may also pose challenges for the industry as a whole. For example, the intense competition among major players could lead to pricing pressures and margin compression, potentially impacting profitability. Furthermore, the growing reliance on complex supply chains and intellectual property could create vulnerabilities in the event of disruptions or cyber attacks.

This satirical cartoon depicts Donald Trump as a giant orange balloon while Xi Jinping calmly prepares to puncture it. The Chinese text roughly means: "No rush, we'll know what to do."
The image captures something that many observers underestimated: Trump appeared convinced that a personal meeting with Xi Jinping could quickly untangle the tariff war and lead to a breakthrough. The assumption seemed to be that pressure, unpredictability and direct leader-to-leader diplomacy would force Beijing toward concessions.
China, however, has often approached strategic competition differently: with patience, long-term calculations and the willingness to absorb short-term costs if larger objectives are at stake.
The message of the cartoon is not really about tariffs alone. It suggests a broader warning: believing complex geopolitical and economic rivalries can be solved through a single handshake may itself become the biggest illusion.
